details.label: Summary
details.text: Intense supercells will remain capable of producing mainly large to very large hail (up to 2-3.5 inches and diameter) this evening as they track east-southeastward

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A supercell which developed over the Black Hills earlier this afternoon strengthened and produced large hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter in southwest SD. Since then, additional supercells have developed over far southeast MT into northwest SD, and over the Black Hills. The environment across western SD remains quite favorable for the maintenance for intense supercells this evening, with strong instability and deep-layer shear both present. These supercells are expected to generally track east-southeastward while posing a threat for mainly large to very large hail up to 2.5-3.5 inches in diameter. Some risk for severe/damaging winds will also exist with RFD surges with these intense cells

details.label: Summary
details.text: Thunderstorms developing along and behind an outflow boundary may pose a transient risk for large hail and/or severe gusts over the next couple of hours. However, these storms will likely remain within an environment unfavorable for substantial intensification and a prolonged severe threat

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Latest surface observations and radar/visible imagery depict an outflow boundary rapidly expanding westward as the cold pool associated with a robust MCS continues to expand. Across southwest IN, an organized, but compact MCS, southwest of Indianapolis has shown steadily declining velocities behind a bowing segment, suggesting that the complex is gradually weakening as it migrates further east into the cold pool. Additionally, new convection continues to develop along and behind the outflow boundary across northern KY. In general, this activity has exhibited transient intensification as buoyant parcels originating within the warm sector are quickly displaced into the cold pool. This trend should generally continue over the next couple of hours with most model solutions hinting at additional thunderstorm development through roughly 00-02 UTC. Storm motions into the cool/stable air mass should continue to limit storm longevity, but strong deep-layer wind shear across may support periodic storm organization with an attendant threat for large hail (most likely around 1 inch) and severe/damaging gusts. Although new watch issuance will likely not be needed, local expansions may be required as new convection emerges

details.label: Summary
details.text: Trends are being monitored for watch issuance soon with widely spaced supercells that have developed this afternoon. Very large hail and severe gusts may occur with this activity

details.label: Discussion
details.text: An intense supercell has developed over far southeast MT along/near a front extending eastward from a weak surface low near KBIL, with a separate supercell having also recently developed over south-central ND near the surface boundary. While surface temperatures are not overly warm (generally in the 80s), modifying the 18Z observed BIS sounding for current conditions suggests minimal MLCIN is present along/south of the boundary in southern ND. Enhanced mid-level west-northwesterly flow across the northern Plains is supporting 40-50 kt of deep-layer shear, which will continue to support supercells in the near term. Mid-level lapse rates around 7.6 C/km in the 700-500 mb layer observed on the 18Z BIS sounding and seasonably cool temperatures aloft have fostered moderate to strong instability across southern ND (MLCAPE around 2000-3000 J/kg). Very large hail potentially up to 2-3 inches in diameter will be possible with any sustained supercell, and storm splitting appears probable given the strong westerly deep-layer shear present/nearly straight mid-level hodographs observed. Occasional severe gusts may also occur as low-level lapse rates steepen further. Given ongoing convection, and the potential for additional activity to develop/move eastward into southwest ND from southeast MT, watch issuance is being considered soon

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A severe MCS continues to push south/southeast across northeastern KY with a history of recently producing winds within the line between 55-65 mph based on reports/wind observations. The peak of the bowing segment continues to align with the intersection of the MCS and a residual outflow boundary/frontal zone draped southward from eastern KY into the southern Appalachians. To the west of this boundary, a very buoyant air mass remains in place and will continue to support the potential for intense convection and severe gusts over the next couple of hours as the line approaches the southern edge of WW 568. Beyond roughly 00 UTC, the general expectation is for the MCS to begin weakening with time as it moves into an air mass that has already seen some degree of convective overturning and into a region with weaker deep-layer wind shear. However, given the well-established cold pool and some residual buoyancy, it appears likely that this weakening trend will be gradual with some lingering threat for severe/damaging wind gusts. Additional downstream watch issuance will likely be needed in the next hour or two to address this potential

mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: Thunderstorms which have developed on a weak surface boundary this afternoon may pose an isolated threat for severe hail/gusts. However, watch issuance is unlikely at this time

details.label: Summary
details.text: Thunderstorms which have developed on a weak surface boundary this afternoon may pose an isolated threat for severe hail/gusts. However, watch issuance is unlikely at this time

details.label: Discussion
details.text: 21Z surface observations and recent visible satellite imagery show a weak surface boundary draped from the NE Panhandle into parts of southwest/south-central NE. While large-scale ascent remains nebulous/weak across this region, modest low-level convergence along the boundary has been sufficient for widely spaced thunderstorm development as convective temperatures have been breached (surface temperatures in the mid 90s to low 100s). Modifying the 18Z LBF sounding for current surface observations suggest MLCIN has become minimal near this boundary, with ample MLCAPE to support robust updrafts. Furthermore, modest low-level winds veer to westerly and strengthen with height through mid-levels (reference recent KLNX VWP), which will support sufficient deep-layer shear for organized updrafts. Ongoing high-based convection may pose a threat for both isolated severe hail and gusty downdraft winds. Still, cooler surface temperatures to the east of the boundary in NE suggest the presence of stronger MLCIN with eastward extent, and it remains unclear whether additional thunderstorms will develop/move off the boundary given nebulous large-scale forcing. Therefore, expectations are for the overall severe threat to remain fairly isolated, and watch issuance appears unlikely at this time
